narrative:
The model estimates you have a 13% chance of failing your final year. While this is not a high probability, it is enough for the school to require you to take remedial courses as a precaution.

The prediction is driven mainly by three aspects of your situation. The most influential factor is that you have had no past class failures. Surprisingly, this actually pushes the model toward expecting you to fail. Among students who passed, zero failures is the average, yet in your specific combination of circumstances the model interprets the lack of prior setbacks as a warning sign rather than a strength. 

The second most important element is your strong desire to pursue higher education. This works in your favor and pulls the prediction toward passing. Almost every student who passed also wanted to continue studying, so this is a solid positive point in your profile.

The third key factor is your limited weekly study time of less than two hours. This pulls the prediction toward failing. Only 21% of students who passed studied this little, while most successful students spent two to five hours or more.

To improve, you should focus on increasing your study time in a consistent way. Even modest extra hours each week, combined with your clear ambition for higher education, could noticeably raise your chances of passing and potentially remove the need for remedial courses.
